description: English Year 4 width tiers — all 28 descriptors. ACARA v9.
subject: English

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor that satisfies the command term of the descriptor. For concept/language standards (LA, LY01, LY09-11): minimum phenomena or contexts. For capability standards (LE, LY02-07): narrowest single task context that meets the verb. For LY08 (handwriting): narrowest motor performance that meets the descriptor.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope grounded in the most common elaboration cases. What a well-taught Year 4 class would have engaged with across the year.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new phenomena or task contexts — not harder versions of the same. At least one First Nations Australian direction included where elaborations indicate. 'Limited width' notes used where genuine breadth is thin (LY08). 2-4 directions per standard.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA v9 elaborations preserved verbatim as source data. Wider directions are derived from and extend beyond elaborations where appropriate. Where no elaborations exist (LY08), depth_fallback is used.

AC9E4LA01.minimum_width: Identify formal and informal language in a provided scenario and explain that language adjusts depending on the situation.
AC9E4LA01.typical_width: Explore how language varies across formal and informal contexts — group discussion vs group report, playground vs classroom, peer vs teacher — identifying specific features (vocabulary, tone, sentence type) that signal formality. Understand how age, expertise and familiarity between participants shape language choices. Recognise inclusive language as a relational choice.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian protocols for greeting Elders and acknowledging Country, comparing these conventions with formal greeting practices in other cultural groups represented in the class community
Compare greeting and address conventions across a range of cultural contexts, explaining what each reveals about cultural values and relationships
Investigate how digital communication contexts (email, chat, social media) sit on the formality spectrum and what signals register in each
Compare formal and informal written registers in the same genre (e.g. formal letter vs text message for the same request) and identify the specific features that mark each
elaborations: recognising that language is adjusted in different contexts; for example, in degree of formality when moving between group discussions and presenting a group report
understanding how age, expertise and familiarity influence the ways in which people interact and how these codes and conventions vary across cultures
recognising the importance of using inclusive language
exploring cultural respects for First Nations Australian Elders, and greeting conventions between First Nations Australians

AC9E4LA02.minimum_width: Identify thinking verbs (e.g. 'I think', 'I believe') as signals of opinion and summary verbs (e.g. 'we concluded') as signals of factual reporting in provided examples.
AC9E4LA02.typical_width: Identify a range of subjective language features (thinking verbs, emotive vocabulary, evaluative adjectives) and objective language features (summary verbs, precise nouns, impersonal constructions) across texts from different curriculum areas, explaining the different purpose each register serves.
wider: Analyse how opinion pieces, reviews and arguments use subjective language strategically alongside objective evidence, and discuss why the mix of registers is deliberate

Compare how the same information is presented in an objective report versus a subjective account (e.g. a scientific finding in a journal versus in a personal blog) and evaluate the effect on the reader
Examine how First Nations Australian authors use subjective voice to position readers in relation to cultural knowledge and experience
elaborations: identifying ways thinking verbs are used to express opinions; for example, "I think", "I believe", and ways summary verbs are used to report findings; for example, "we concluded"
comparing statements that have similar information presented objectively and subjectively; for example, "The man has 6 cats." "The man has too many noisy cats."

AC9E4LA03.minimum_width: Identify the stages of one familiar text type and explain the purpose of each stage.
AC9E4LA03.typical_width: Identify and describe the characteristic stages and key language features of at least four text types from different curriculum areas — including narratives, information reports, sequential and causal explanations, and arguments — explaining how stage organisation and language features together serve each text's social purpose. Distinguish text form (poster, email) from stage organisation.
wider: Compare how the same social purpose (e.g. persuading) is achieved through different stage structures across different text types — argument, advertisement, speech — identifying what stage structures are shared and what differs
Examine how digital text forms adapt or modify traditional stage structures, and how multimodal texts use visual stages alongside verbal stages
Explore how First Nations Australian storytelling forms organise stages differently from Western narrative structures, and discuss how purpose and cultural context shape these differences
Compare stage structures in sequential versus causal explanations and in comparative versus part-whole information reports, explaining why the content determines the structure
elaborations: identifying the typical stages and language features of texts such as narratives, factual recounts, imaginative recounts, biographies, information reports, explanations, book talks, poetry and arguments for a particular purpose
understanding how and why text structure is important in texts such as sequential and causal explanations, and comparative and part-whole information reports

recognising that poems have different purposes that influence the organisation into characteristic stages; for example, poems that tell stories, poems that describe and poems that reflect on aspects of life
recognising the difference between a text's form such as a poster, email or list and its organisation into stages depending on its social purpose

AC9E4LA04.minimum_width: Identify a text connective in a sentence and name the type of relationship it signals (e.g. contrast, sequence, cause).
AC9E4LA04.typical_width: Identify and explain the cohesive role of a range of text connectives — temporal (firstly, then, finally), adversative (however, nevertheless), causal (therefore, as a result), additive (in addition, furthermore) — and pronouns and determiners (this, that, these, those) across informational and narrative texts, explaining how each device maintains coherence.
wider: Compare how temporal connectives are used in sequential explanation texts versus narrative recounts, explaining how the text type shapes connective choice
Compare how causal connectives function in argument texts versus scientific explanations, identifying differences in the logical relationships they signal
Examine how First Nations Australian oral narrative traditions use temporal sequencing in storytelling, comparing with written sequential texts
Analyse how cohesion breaks down in texts where pronoun reference is unclear, revising to restore it
elaborations: recognising how authors construct texts that are cohesive and coherent using pronouns that link to something previously mentioned and determiners; for example, "this", "that", "these" and "those", to identify things
recognising how authors use text connectives to create links between sentences; for example, "however", "therefore", "nevertheless" and "in addition"
recognising how text connectives link sections of a text, providing sequences through time; for example, "firstly", "then", "next" and "finally"

AC9E4LA05.minimum_width: Identify two navigation features specific to online texts (e.g. hyperlinks, drop-down menus) and explain how each helps a reader.
AC9E4LA05.typical_width: Compare navigation features in print texts (headings, subheadings, table of contents) with online equivalents (home pages, subpages, hyperlinks, drop-down menus, graphics, layout) across two or more websites, explaining how online features support reader selection and navigation of content for a purpose.
wider: Compare navigation features across two websites on similar topics (e.g. two science information sites for students) and evaluate which is more effective for a reader and why
Design a navigation structure for a hypothetical webpage on a familiar topic and explain the purpose of each feature chosen
elaborations: investigating the features used for texts such as headings and subheadings in print text, home pages and subpages in digital texts, and how these help the reader select text for a purpose
comparing the features of texts on similar topics online

AC9E4LA06.minimum_width: Identify the independent and dependent clauses in a complex sentence and name the subordinating conjunction that joins them.
AC9E4LA06.typical_width: Identify and explain independent and dependent clauses across a range of complex sentences — including fronted dependent clauses — naming the subordinating conjunction and the relationship type it creates (time, cause, condition, concession, manner). Create complex sentences using dependent clauses to add circumstantial information.
wider: Compare how complex sentences with temporal versus causal subordination are used differently in narrative texts versus explanation texts, explaining how text type shapes syntactic choice
Examine how the position of the dependent clause (fronted vs final) changes emphasis in a complex sentence, using examples from texts in different curriculum areas
Revise a piece of writing to replace simple sentences with complex sentences and evaluate the effect on precision and readability
elaborations: creating richer, more specific sentences by including information about place, time, manner, cause or condition in a dependent clause; for example, "Denise found a cocoon." becomes "Denise decided to keep an eye on the cocoon until the butterfly emerged."
creating more precise and detailed sentences by adding adverbial clauses; for example, "They crossed the mountain range." becomes "Although the path was overgrown, they crossed the mountain range."

AC9E4LA07.minimum_width: Identify direct and indirect speech in provided examples and name two features that distinguish them.
AC9E4LA07.typical_width: Identify direct and indirect speech across narrative and non-narrative texts, explaining the grammatical features of each (quotation marks, saying verbs, tense shift, pronoun change) and why a writer chooses one over the other depending on purpose — authenticity and character in narrative; efficiency and attribution in reporting.
wider: Compare how direct speech is used in narrative (to reveal character and create immediacy) versus news reporting (to attribute claims), explaining how purpose drives the choice
Transform a passage between direct and indirect speech and evaluate how the change affects tone, authenticity and reader experience
Examine how dialogue in First Nations Australian literary texts uses direct speech to convey voice, community and cultural perspective
Investigate how reported speech can shift meaning or emphasis, and discuss implications for fairness in journalistic and historical reporting
elaborations: investigating examples of quoted (direct) speech; for example, "He said, 'I'll go to the park today.'" and reported (indirect) speech; for example, "He told me he was going to the park today." and why they have been used in different contexts

AC9E4LA08.minimum_width: Identify an adverb phrase or prepositional phrase in a sentence and name the type of circumstantial detail it provides (time, place, manner or cause).
AC9E4LA08.typical_width: Identify adverb groups/phrases and prepositional phrases providing different types of circumstantial detail — time, place, manner, cause — across literary and informational texts, explaining how stacking multiple phrases builds richly circumstantiated description.
wider: Compare how circumstantial phrases are used in literary texts (for atmosphere and imagery) versus scientific descriptions (for precision and replicability), explaining how purpose drives the choice

Collect examples of prepositional phrases from texts in different curriculum areas and analyse which types of circumstantial detail predominate in each (e.g. manner in science, time in recounts, place in geography)
Experiment with placing adverb and prepositional phrases in different positions in a sentence and evaluate how placement changes emphasis
elaborations: investigating in texts how adverb groups/phrases and prepositional phrases can provide details of the circumstances surrounding a happening or state; for example, "At midnight (time) he rose slowly (manner) from the chair (place) and went upstairs (place)."

AC9E4LA09.minimum_width: Identify the tense of at least three sentences and name the verb form used in each.
AC9E4LA09.typical_width: Identify past, present and future tense across a range of text types and explain why each text type is typically written in a particular tense — informative texts in present, recounts in past, procedures in imperative/present. Identify tense shifts within texts and explain why they occur.
wider: Examine a text that mixes tenses (e.g. a biography moving between past narrative and present reflection) and explain the purpose of each tense shift
Compare tense use in First Nations Australian storytelling texts, considering how tense relates to the living nature of story in oral traditions compared with written texts
Compare tense use across informational texts from different curriculum areas (science, HASS, maths) and identify whether tense conventions vary by discipline
elaborations: understanding the tense that types of texts are commonly written in; for example, informative texts are usually written in present tense
identifying the tense in texts they read

AC9E4LA10.minimum_width: Identify the framing of an image (close-up, mid or wide shot) and explain one effect on the viewer. Identify the most salient element and give one reason why it stands out.
AC9E4LA10.typical_width: Analyse how framing choices, element placement (foreground/background, centre/margin) and salience (size, colour, focus, contrast) work together across a range of still and moving images to direct viewer attention and create meaning, using metalanguage (framing, composition, salience) to describe choices.
wider: Compare image composition across different cultural contexts, including how First Nations Australian visual art uses composition and salience differently from Western photographic and illustrative conventions
Analyse how moving images use camera movement and editing to create dynamic salience across time, comparing with the fixed composition of still images
Compare how the same subject photographed with different framings creates different emotional responses, using a sequence of images as evidence
Examine how image composition in advertising positions the viewer in relation to the product, using framing, placement and salience deliberately
elaborations: examining visual and multimodal texts, building a vocabulary to describe visual elements and techniques such as framing, composition and salience, and beginning to understand how these choices influence viewer response

AC9E4LA11.minimum_width: Identify two synonyms for a word and explain one difference in meaning or connotation. Identify the antonym of a word and explain how the contrast clarifies meaning.
AC9E4LA11.typical_width: Explore synonym clusters across vocabulary from a range of curriculum areas, explaining shades of meaning (intensity, formality, connotation) and selecting precise synonyms for context. Identify antonym pairs and explain how contrast creates emphasis. Use new vocabulary encountered in a range of sources — including technical, learning-area and First Nations Australian vocabulary — in own speaking and writing.
wider: Research words from First Nations Australian languages used in Australian English — including place names, flora and fauna terms — and explore their origins and meanings
Build synonym clusters for key vocabulary from a current cross-curriculum topic (e.g. science, HASS) and compare shades of meaning to make precise word choices in writing
Investigate how antonym pairs are used in persuasive texts to create contrast between positions and evaluate the rhetorical effect
Create a personal vocabulary reference organised by topic, collecting new words from cross-curriculum reading with synonyms, antonyms and example sentences
elaborations: building vocabulary from research about technical and learning area-specific topics; for example, gravity and magnetic forces
determining or clarifying the shades of meaning of synonyms and antonyms

using words encountered in texts that are formed from a First Nations Australian language; for example, Woomba Woomba or Toowoom was the place referred to by First Nations Australians on the Darling Downs and then the name was referred to as Toowoomba by the drovers

AC9E4LA12.minimum_width: Punctuate a basic dialogue sentence correctly using quotation marks, capital letter for the spoken words and appropriate boundary punctuation.
AC9E4LA12.typical_width: Identify and apply all dialogue punctuation conventions across a range of dialogue patterns — speech first with said tag, said tag first, speech interrupted by said tag — explaining the purpose of each convention (quotation marks enclose exact words; comma before said tag; capital opens spoken words; boundary punctuation inside quotation marks).
wider: Analyse how published authors use dialogue punctuation for pace — short rapid exchanges versus longer speeches — and identify how punctuation choices support each
Compare dialogue punctuation conventions across a range of published Australian texts (single vs double quotation marks, punctuation style variations) and discuss conventions
Edit a piece of dialogue with multiple punctuation errors, explaining each correction made
elaborations: identifying the use of quotation marks, capital letters, commas and boundary punctuation to signal dialogue in texts
using punctuated dialogue in own writing

AC9E4LE01.minimum_width: Identify a similar storyline pattern across two texts from different cultural contexts and explain what makes them similar.
AC9E4LE01.typical_width: Identify recurring storyline patterns — journey, transformation, conflict and resolution, coming-of-age — across at least three texts from different cultural contexts including at least one First Nations Australian text. Identify themes and connect them to personal experience, other texts and the wider world. Explain how cultural context shapes character, setting and relationship portrayals even when the underlying pattern is familiar.
wider: Investigate how a universal storyline pattern (e.g. the hero's journey) appears in First Nations Australian, European and Asian literary traditions, comparing how cultural context shapes the same underlying pattern
Explore how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors portray characters through relationship with Country and community, and how this differs from individualised Western character development
Compare how a theme (e.g. belonging, courage, loss) is treated differently across texts from diverse cultural contexts and discuss what each treatment reveals about cultural values
Read texts by the same author and track how recurring storyline patterns and character relationships appear across their body of work
elaborations: making connections with similar storylines and ideas across texts for a range of cultural contexts
identifying the themes in literary texts, and connecting these to own experience, other texts and the wider world
exploring the connection between characters and settings as aspects of the narrative in books from the same author

AC9E4LE02.minimum_width: Identify one structural feature and one language feature in a literary text, name each using metalanguage, and describe the effect of one on the reader.
AC9E4LE02.typical_width: Identify and discuss the effects of a range of structural choices (chapter structure, flashback, circular ending) and language features (repetition, figurative language, dialogue, tense choices) across literary texts, using metalanguage and connecting specific features to specific reader effects. Share opinions about texts with text-referenced support.
wider: Compare how the same structural or language feature (e.g. repetition, circular structure) produces different effects in two different texts, explaining why context changes the effect
Respond to a First Nations Australian literary text using metalanguage to describe structural and language features, with attention to how cultural context shapes interpretive choices
Write a short alternative version of a passage using different structural or language choices and describe how the effect changes
Compare personal response to a text with a peer's, identifying where opinions differ and examining which textual features each reader is prioritising
elaborations: building on personal responses by identifying and describing how authors and illustrators use language and visual features to create meaning
using metalanguage to discuss the effects of text structures and language features on personal and literary response

AC9E4LE03.minimum_width: Identify two techniques an author uses to develop a character and name the mood created by a setting in a literary text. Identify the main conflict and one tension-building technique.
AC9E4LE03.typical_width: Discuss how authors develop characters through dialogue, action, direct description, narrator commentary and other characters' reactions. Explain how setting choices — time, weather, sensory detail, colour — create mood. Analyse how plot tension is built through conflict types, pacing and structural choices (cliffhangers, chapter endings, delayed resolution) and explain the connections between character, setting and tension.
wider: Compare how character is developed differently across picture books (illustration and sparse text) and chapter books (extended description and dialogue), explaining how format shapes technique
Examine how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors portray Country as an active participant in setting and mood, comparing with Western landscape description in texts on similar themes
Map the tension curve of a literary text, identifying moments of rising tension, release and climax, and analyse the structural choices that create this shape
Compare how tension is built using different techniques across two texts in the same genre, identifying shared techniques and author-specific choices
elaborations: identifying and examining how authors develop characters through what characters say, think and do as well as through how they are described by the narrator or other characters
examining the connection between setting and mood by identifying authors' and illustrators' choices of language and visual features

AC9E4LE04.minimum_width: Identify one example each of figurative language (simile, personification or alliteration) and explain the effect it creates. Identify a pun or deliberate word play and explain the double meaning.
AC9E4LE04.typical_width: Examine how figurative language (simile, personification, alliteration), deliberate word play (puns, ambiguity) and rhythm work across poetry and literary texts to produce specific effects — comparison, animation, sound pattern, humour, multiple meaning, pace — explaining the deliberate choice behind each device.
wider: Examine figurative language in First Nations Australian poetry, including how imagery draws on Country, seasonal cycles and cultural knowledge for its effects, and compare with imagery in other poetic traditions
Compare how the same figurative device (e.g. simile) is used for contrasting effects in two different texts — one creating beauty, one creating threat or humour
Compare the rhythm of a traditional children's poem with a contemporary free-verse poem, explaining how different rhythmic choices produce different reading experiences
Collect examples of deliberate word play from a range of sources (poetry, advertisements, books) and categorise by type and effect, explaining the author's choice in each case
elaborations: discussing the effect of literary devices such as similes, personification, and alliteration in poetry and literary texts
discussing word play such as puns, jokes, and deliberate use of ambiguity and recognising the deliberate choices behind their use

AC9E4LE05.minimum_width: Create a literary text with a planned structure, correctly punctuated dialogue and at least one literary device. Give and receive one piece of specific peer feedback and make at least one revision.
AC9E4LE05.typical_width: Plan, create and edit literary texts by making deliberate choices about storyline structure, character development techniques and setting with mood. Use a range of sentence types, dialogue and literary devices with intentional effect. Engage in structured peer editing focused on storyline, character and setting choices, and revise the text substantively in response to feedback.
wider: Create literary texts in different forms — narrative, prose poem, short story, picture book — and compare how the same story content is shaped differently by each form
Create a literary text inspired by First Nations Australian storytelling structures or imagery, with attention to respectful and informed use of cultural elements
Use a published author's revision process (from interviews, craft books or manuscript facsimiles) as a model for own editing approach
Compare a first draft and revised version, annotating specific changes and explaining the reason for each improvement made
elaborations: creating texts using a range of sentence types, including dialogue and literary devices
collaborating with a peer to edit literary texts by sharing feedback about choices made to develop storylines, characters and settings

AC9E4LY01.minimum_width: Identify two texts from different time periods with the same purpose and describe one similarity and one difference in how they depict events.
AC9E4LY01.typical_width: Compare texts from at least two different time periods across multiple dimensions — language choices, visual conventions, what is included or excluded, whose perspective is represented — explaining how the historical context of each text shapes the depiction.
wider: Compare news coverage or documentary footage of the same type of event (e.g. a major sporting event) from different decades, examining how depictions have changed and what this reveals about changing values

Compare how First Nations Australian events or stories have been depicted in texts made at different periods, discussing whose perspective was represented and how this has changed as more First Nations voices have been included
Compare family communication texts (letters, postcards, emails, text messages) across different periods and explain how technology has changed form while purpose remains similar
elaborations: viewing documentaries and news footage from different periods, comparing the purpose and audience; for example, coverage of major sporting events
comparing the texts used to communicate between family members, noting similarities and differences as a result of changing technology

AC9E4LY02.minimum_width: Listen to a peer's contribution, identify one key point and use an acknowledgement phrase ('I agree with... because...' or 'I see it differently because...') in a follow-up response.
AC9E4LY02.typical_width: Listen actively in discussions, tracking key points and information, and contribute using a range of discussion language that acknowledges, extends, questions and links contributions. Make notes about tasks, ask clarifying questions and present ideas clearly and coherently.
wider: Practise discussion skills in structured formats (Socratic seminar, fishbowl, think-pair-share) where referencing others' ideas and extending contributions is explicitly required
Compare formal discussion language conventions across different contexts (class meeting, debate, book club discussion) and explain how the context affects language choices
Reflect on own listening and discussion contribution after a structured discussion, identifying what was effective and what could be improved
elaborations: making notes about a task, asking questions to clarify or follow up information, and seeking assistance if required
developing speaking and listening behaviours including acknowledging and extending others' contributions, presenting ideas and opinions clearly and coherently

AC9E4LY03.minimum_width: Identify two characteristic features of one text type (imaginative, informative or persuasive) and explain how each helps the text achieve its purpose.
AC9E4LY03.typical_width: Identify and explain the characteristic language, visual and structural features of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts — including descriptive and figurative language in imaginative texts; headings, diagrams and topic sentences in informative texts; emotive language, rhetorical questions and evidence in persuasive texts — explaining how each feature serves the text's purpose.
wider: Compare characteristic features across two different persuasive text types (e.g. argument essay and advertisement) and identify which features are shared and which are genre-specific
Examine how First Nations Australian imaginative texts use features that reflect oral storytelling traditions and cultural knowledge, comparing with Western narrative conventions
Compare informative text features across digital and print formats, identifying what features are shared and what the digital medium adds or changes
Analyse how multimodal texts combine language and visual features to create meaning in each of the three text types
elaborations: identifying how authors use language to create imaginary worlds
identifying how authors use techniques, such as headings, italics and bold text, to support readers or viewers to navigate specific texts
identifying visual features such as images and layout used in informative texts to complement, add to or shape understanding of a topic

AC9E4LY04.minimum_width: Explain what each of the three knowledge sources does for a reader and demonstrate one self-correction strategy when reading a challenging text.
AC9E4LY04.typical_width: Read different text types accurately and fluently by integrating phonic, semantic and grammatical knowledge simultaneously, applying self-correction strategies — re-reading, pausing, cross-checking — when meaning breaks down, across a range of curriculum texts including subject-specific language.
wider: Apply integrated reading strategies to increasingly complex subject-specific texts from science, HASS and maths, reflecting on which knowledge source most often requires activation
Analyse what goes wrong when only one knowledge source is applied (e.g. phonically correct but semantically wrong word choice) and explain how cross-checking corrects this
Reflect on own reading profile using the three knowledge sources as a framework, identifying relative strengths and areas for development
elaborations: reading increasingly complex texts using established word identification strategies, knowledge of the topic and understanding of text structure and language features

AC9E4LY05.minimum_width: Identify the main idea and two supporting details in an informational text. Use one named inference strategy to explain a meaning not directly stated. Write a brief summary in own words.
AC9E4LY05.typical_width: Apply the full repertoire of named comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring and questioning — to build literal and inferred meaning across a range of text types. Evaluate texts by assessing evidence quality, argument strength and representation, with text-referenced reasoning.
wider: Apply comprehension strategies to multimodal texts, connecting meaning across verbal, visual and sound modes — including texts by First Nations Australian authors and illustrators where colours, images, symbols and patterns carry cultural meaning
Evaluate how First Nations Australian perspectives are represented (or misrepresented) in texts, using criteria of fairness, accuracy and whose voice is heard
Compare evaluations of the same text from two different readers and discuss how different values or prior knowledge lead to different evaluations
Apply inference and monitoring strategies to complex subject-specific texts from other curriculum areas, reflecting on how discipline language affects comprehension
elaborations: making connections between information in print, images and sound
reading or listening for key topic-specific vocabulary words to build understanding
reading or listening to interpret the main idea and supporting ideas
identifying evidence and reasoning used by authors to support points or arguments
applying self-monitoring strategies such as re-reading, pausing and questioning, and self-correction strategies such as confirming and cross-checking
connecting the use of colours, images, symbols and patterns in texts by First Nations Australian authors and illustrators
evaluating an author's use of evidence to support arguments

AC9E4LY06.minimum_width: Plan and create a text in one text type using at least one complex sentence and one text connective. Edit for at least one vocabulary improvement and one spelling check.
AC9E4LY06.typical_width: Plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts across all three text types — imaginative, informative and persuasive — using visual features, complex sentences, text connectives for cohesion, appropriate tense, topic-specific vocabulary with synonyms and antonyms, correct multisyllabic word spelling and consistent simple punctuation. Revise for vocabulary precision and cohesion.
wider: Create texts in two different text types on the same topic and compare how structure, sentence type and vocabulary choices change to suit each purpose
Create a multimodal text that integrates verbal and visual elements to communicate linked ideas, explaining how visual features complement the written content
Use digital writing and publishing tools to create and refine a text, and compare the editing process with handwritten drafting
Research and integrate information from multiple sources including online sources into an informative or persuasive text, with attention to paraphrasing and acknowledgement
elaborations: using research to gather ideas for writing and integrating information from a range of sources which may include those found online
selecting text structure and planning how to group ideas into paragraphs to sequence content
using topic-specific, precise and varied vocabulary
using grammatical features including different types of verb groups, noun groups and adverb groups/phrases for effective descriptions and details according to purpose
revising written texts to improve the selection of words used to connect ideas and improve the cohesion of the text

AC9E4LY07.minimum_width: Plan and deliver a structured presentation on one topic using at least one complex sentence and one deliberate voice feature (pace, volume, pitch or tone varied for effect).
AC9E4LY07.typical_width: Plan, create, rehearse and deliver structured oral and/or multimodal presentations across a range of purposes — report, story, recount, argument — using appropriate language register (subjective or objective), complex sentences, integrated visual features and deliberate voice control (tone, pace, pitch, volume). Rehearse with a peer, receive specific feedback and make adjustments.
wider: Deliver the same content in two different presentation contexts (formal classroom vs informal small group) and reflect on how delivery choices change across contexts
Create and deliver a multimodal presentation combining spoken language with slides, images or props, explaining how visual and verbal elements complement each other
Deliver a presentation incorporating First Nations Australian content with attention to respectful language choices and appropriate acknowledgement conventions
Compare own delivery with a recording, evaluating voice features against the criteria practised in rehearsal
elaborations: reporting on a topic in an organised manner, providing relevant facts and descriptive detail to support audience understanding, and using references to reliable sources to support claims
exploring the effects of changing tone, volume, pitch and pace in formal and informal contexts
choosing a variety of appropriate words and phrases, including descriptive words and some technical vocabulary, to communicate meaning accurately
rehearsing a presentation with a peer and sharing feedback about tone, pace, pitch and volume appropriate to audience

AC9E4LY08.minimum_width: Write a short piece using joined letters that are legible and consistently formed.
AC9E4LY08.typical_width: Write extended pieces across a range of tasks using clearly formed joined letters with developing fluency, so that handwriting does not impede composition.
wider: Limited width — joined handwriting fluency is a motor automaticity target that does not vary meaningfully across contexts at this year band. Extension involves writing at greater length and speed while maintaining legibility, not broadening application. Practice volume is the operative variable.
AC9E4LY08.width_notes: depth_fallback used: AC9E4LY08 has no elaborations. Handwriting automaticity is a motor skill — genuine breadth does not exist. Extension goes further in fluency and length, not across new contexts.

AC9E4LY09.minimum_width: Apply knowledge of complex vowel patterns to read and write at least five multisyllabic words correctly, including words with unstressed vowels. Identify a prefix or suffix and use it to decode or spell a related word.
AC9E4LY09.typical_width: Apply phonological and morphological knowledge to read and write multisyllabic words with a range of complex letter combinations — including unstressed vowels, vowel digraphs in multisyllabic words, and known prefixes and suffixes — explaining how the knowledge helps with both decoding and spelling.
wider: Sort multisyllabic words by vowel pattern and identify generalisations that predict spelling, noting exceptions
Explore how the same prefix or suffix appears across multiple word families and generalise about its meaning contribution (e.g. -ful: careful, thankful, hopeful)
Use morphological decomposition as a reading strategy for unfamiliar long words in subject-area texts, explaining the process used
elaborations: recognising unstressed vowels in multisyllabic words and how these vowel sounds are written; for example, "builder" and "animal"
using phonic and morphemic knowledge to read and write multisyllabic words with more complex letter combinations; for example, "straightaway" and "thoughtful"

AC9E4LY10.minimum_width: Apply one spelling generalisation (e.g. doubling rule when adding -ing) to at least three words correctly and name the rule. Build a word family of at least three members from a base word.
AC9E4LY10.typical_width: Apply a range of spelling generalisations — doubling rules, drop-e rules, change-y-to-i rules — across common affixes. Build and explore morphological word families, using family relationships as a spelling strategy. Explore word origins from Latin and Greek roots to understand how roots generate word families.
wider: Explore word families from Latin and Greek roots (e.g. tri-: tricycle, tripod, triangle; port-: transport, portable, import) and identify how knowing the root helps spell and define multiple words across curriculum areas
Research the word families of key vocabulary from a current cross-curriculum unit (e.g. science, HASS) and use family knowledge to spell and define related forms
Investigate which spelling generalisations have exceptions and explore etymological reasons why (e.g. words of French or Latin origin may follow different patterns)
elaborations: applying generalisations for adding affixes; for example, "hope" – "hoping", "begin" – "beginning", "country" – "countries"
building morphemic word families and exploring word origins; for example, "tricycle", "tripod" and "triangle"

AC9E4LY11.minimum_width: Name at least three homophone pairs, explain the different meaning of each word in two pairs, and select the correct homophone in at least three sentences using context clues.
AC9E4LY11.typical_width: Identify a range of common homophone pairs (our/hour, their/there/they're, to/too/two, hear/here, wear/ware/where) and apply contextual and syntactical clues systematically to select the correct spelling in sentences and own writing, explaining the reasoning used.
wider: Investigate near-homophones and commonly confused words (e.g. affect/effect, then/than, its/it's) and develop memory strategies or rules for distinguishing them
Edit a piece of writing specifically for homophone errors, explaining the reasoning for each correction
Examine how homophone errors in published or digital texts change meaning and discuss the importance of proofreading for homophones specifically
elaborations: recognising that contextual and syntactical clues can be used to determine the use of homophones; for example, "We grow wheat on our farm." "The train trip will take about an hour."
